I would stay with the standard Quzhou pattern and plant the same land in a winter wheat and summer maize rotation. In my county, that system fits the weather, the water pattern, and the way I can manage labor. Most of the rain comes in summer, so maize fits the rainy season well, and wheat is still the crop I trust through winter and spring if I can give it a few irrigations. I would not spread myself across too many crops, because that adds risk, makes field work less timely, and is harder for me to manage well. I would rather do one familiar rotation properly than chase a higher price crop and lose control of water, weeds, or timing.

I would use improved seed for wheat and hybrid seed for maize. For wheat, I would keep fertilizer moderate but steady, with nitrogen as the main input, plus phosphorus and potassium so the stand stays balanced and the grain fills better. I would irrigate wheat three times if water is available: once around jointing, once around booting or heading, and once around grain filling if the field is dry. I would plough or rotary-till only as much as needed to get a firm seedbed, control weeds early, and spray only when disease or insects justify it. After wheat harvest, I would move quickly into summer maize on the same land, using no-tillage or very light disturbance so I do not lose moisture or time. Because summer rainfall is stronger here, I would usually irrigate maize once, maybe twice if the rains fail, and I would keep pesticide use lower than in wheat unless insects build up. My goal would be stable grain yield, lower water stress, and a plan I can carry through on time.
